name: Vibrating reducing belt

lead: The vibrating reducing belt is a stand-up machine in which a motor drives a wide fabric belt that is worn or leaned against around the waist, hips or thighs. It was sold from the 1950s as a passive way to break up fat and slim the midsection, and today's portable vibrating belts are marketed the same way.

A look-improvement payoff is the claim: a slimmer waist and firmer stomach. Reference accounts say the devices had been shown by the 1980s not to reduce fat; a 2023 preprint examined local abdominal vibration for waist circumference in overweight women.

paras: Users stand on the platform and lean against the belt to vibrate the target area for a session; modern versions are portable belts worn on the waist and sold via infomercials. Some people use them as a massage tool.

A 2013 case report described bilateral chronic subdural hematoma in a 75-year-old man after using a vibrating belt machine on his own head for 20 days.[1] Standard safety guidance for vibration devices applies.

angle.text: The belt is sold as a way to slim the waist and abdomen without exercise. Users apply it to the waist, hips or thighs for the stated goal of a slimmer outline.

lead: The vibrating belt machine consists of a platform, a waist-high post holding an electric motor, and one or two wide belts; the user leans away from the motor so the belt vibrates the targeted body part.[1] It was promoted in the 1950s and 1960s as a passive way to reduce abdominal fat, and appeared in comedy on television shows of the era.[1]

Early versions came from Swedish physician Gustav Zander in the late nineteenth century as massage devices, and in 1927 John Harvey Kellogg promoted a version, the Battle Creek Health Builder, at his sanitarium.[1] Portable belts such as Vibro Shape later reappeared in infomercials.[1]
Marketers of similar belts, such as Ab Force, were reported to have paid $7 million in 2009 over fitness claims.[2]

paras: The classic machine has a stand-on platform, a motor post and fabric belts attached to the motor; users lean back against the belt.[1]

Versions evolved from Zander's nineteenth-century mechanotherapy through Kellogg's 1927 model to 1950s salon and home reducing machines.[1] Reference accounts say it became clear by the 1980s that the devices had no fat-reducing benefit, and they became a comedic element on TV.[1]

A 2013 case report in the Journal of Korean Neurosurgical Society described a 75-year-old man who developed bilateral chronic subdural hematoma after 20 days of exercising with a vibrating belt machine on his head.[3]

Studies of vibrating belts in medicine concern other purposes: a 2025 randomised crossover trial compared a vibrating belt with a positional pillow for positional sleep apnea in 102 adults.[4] A 2023 preprint examined local abdominal vibration on waist circumference and central obesity in overweight sedentary women.[5]
